newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries higher as balanced budget deal done.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries higher as balanced budget deal done.

text.p: The prices of U.S. Treasury securities were trading higher late Friday, boosted by the announcement of a balanced budget accord.
The positive close was coming following a tug of war between bulls and bears as each culled favorable data out of the April nonfarm payrolls report early in the trading session.

The Labor Department reported that payrolls rose 142,000, but at the same time the unemployment rate dropped below 5.0 percent to 4.9 percent -- its lowest reading in 23 years. Many forecasters were looking for gains of more than 200,000.

"The market got a bid about an hour before (the budget deal) was announced" based on optimism for an agreement and talk that a large institutional investor would buy $4 billion to $5 billion in bonds, said Paul McCulley, chief economist at UBS Securities Inc.
However, McCulley said there was not a lot of trading activity during the afternoon and fiscal policy was really just an overlay to underlying economic fundamentals.
"The bottom line is bond market (movement) is determined by the pace of the economy. The slope of the yield curve may become a little flatter" but nothing was fundamentally changed, he said.

Paul Kasriel, economist at Northern Trust Co., didn't see much positive residual effect for the fixed-income markets with the signing of a budget agreement, though he conceded it was propping up market sentiment.
As importantly, he said there was a growing expectation that the Federal Reserve was not going to further tighten monetary policy at its next meeting on May 20.

"Yes we have a lower unemployment rate, but there is precious little evidence of inflation and we're likely to see weaker numbers between now (and the FOMC)," said Kasriel. Retail sales and industrial production could taper off, he said.
"There is a growing expectation that the Fed will hold its fire on May 20," Kasriel said.

But on the budget agreement, Kasriel said "it's unclear to me that in the short-run (the next year or so) this will be better for the bond market than no agreement. Part of it appears (to be based) on an expectation that the Bureau of Labor Statistics will lower the CPI calculation in the years ahead," Kasriel said.
Labor was going to that regardless of the balanced budget amendment, and some of the concessions Clinton had to fight for would be very consumption oriented -- such as tuition credits, he said.
"With the next set of strong numbers, the market will all about the budget deal," Kasriel said.

The bond market remained in narrow ranges following the announcement of the budget pact. Traders said next week's refunding operation was helping to keep a lid on volatility and pointed to the gains already seen this week as capping upside potential.

The Federal Reserve again intervened in the banking system Friday by adding over the weekend system repurchase agreements. The Fed's add need was seen as remaining strong as tax receipts were higher than they have been in years.
The Treasury's 30-year benchmark was trading at 96-20/32, up 9/32 to yield 6.89 percent.

At the short end of the maturity range, three-month bill rates were up three basis points to 5.10 percent, six-month bill rates were up one basis point at 5.32 percent and year bill rates were unchanged at 5.55 percent.
Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-8/32, yielding 6.24 percent. Five-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-13/32, yielding 6.53 percent. Ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 97-02/32, yielding 6.66 percent.
